newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia blast could herald pre-election violence.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia blast could herald pre-election violence.

text.p: A deadly grenade attack on an opposition rally in the Cambodian capital at the weekend could herald a campaign of violence ahead of general elections expected late next year, analysts said on Monday.

"Yesterday is just the beginning of the violence, I think we will have more from now until the elections," royalist member of parliament Ahmad Yahya said of Sunday's explosions that killed at least 14 outside parliament.

The MP said he believed the attack was aimed at a demonstration organised by Sam Rainsy, leader of the official unrecognised Khmer Nation Party (KNP), and was designed to deter poeople from taking part in anti-government protests organised by the KNP.

"I hope it's not the beginning of a new cycle (of violence and political tension)," said a Western diplomat, adding that as far as he knew it was the worst single act of political violence in Cambodia in more than two decades.
"Democracy in Cambodia is doing a U-turn now," said Ahmad Yahya. Cambodia's image in the region and elsewhere was badly tarnished, he added.
Cambodia hopes later this year to join the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
"It could jeopardise relations with ASEAN...it's a really bad atmosphere," said deputy Om Radmady, who also saw the violence as a warning to the KNP and demonstrators.
Sam Rainsy, who narrowly escaped injury in Sunday's blast, has accused his bitter foe Second Prime Minister Hun Sen of the Cambodian People's Party (CPP) of being behind the attack.

Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition government with the royalist FUNCINPEC party after U.N.-ogranised elections in 1993, has condemned the violence but said that the organisers should be arrested and barred from leaving the country.
Police loyal to the CPP have linked Sam Rainsy to the November 19 murder of Hun Sen's brother-in-law, and warned that he could be called in for questioning.

San Rainsy recently formed a political alliance with FUNCINPEC, marking a rapprochement with the party that had expelled him in 1995 for his criticism of government. They are expected to battle the CPP in next year's polls.
The two leading parties agreed in March that general elections should be held in November 1998, but many analysts worry that the polls will not be free and fair.

"This country is basically falling into anarchy. There's no government, there's just two big parties (CPP and FUNCINPEC) fighting," said a foreign human rights worker. "There's going to be more of the same (violence)."
Some analysts acknowledged the seriousness of the attack and voiced concerns about the violence, but were more optimistic about the future.

"I think it's a good sign that the two prime ministers have let the Interior Ministry committee investigate," said one Asian envoy, referring to the cooperation on the blast follow-up by feuding leaders Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
"Trading of charges and counter-charges is not helpful," he said.

U.S. Ambassador Kenneth Quin said in a statement: "It is imperative that all in Cambodia do everything possible to avoid any future violence which could put at risk the significant progress Cambodia has made in recent years."
